section.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
section.sectionRationale: The Chronicler opens his account of Solomon not with the throne or the palace but with worship: Solomon and all Israel go up to the old tabernacle at Gibeon, and there, before ever a stone of the temple is laid, God appears to him at night. What Solomon asks for, and what God gives in reply, sets the tone for the whole reign that follows.
section.thesis: Solomon's request for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people, rather than riches or honor for himself, pleases the LORD, who grants both the wisdom asked for and the wealth not asked for, showing that those who seek first the LORD's kingdom find every other good thing given besides.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Solomon and all Israel worship at Gibeon, verses 1 to 6; God's offer and Solomon's request, verses 7 to 10; God's answer and gift, verses 11 to 13; and Solomon's resulting wealth and power, verses 14 to 17.

units.label: Solomon and all Israel worship at Gibeon
units.note: before the throne, the tent of meeting

verses.text: Now Solomon son of David established himself securely over his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and highly exalted him.
Then Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel, the heads of the families.
And Solomon and the whole assembly went to the high place at Gibeon because it was the location of God's {{ohel|Tent of Meeting}}, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness.
Now David had brought the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, because he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.
But the bronze altar made by Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, was in Gibeon before the tabernacle of the LORD. So Solomon and the assembly inquired of Him there.
Solomon offered sacrifices there before the LORD on the bronze altar at the Tent of Meeting, where he offered a thousand burnt offerings.

units.label: God's offer and Solomon's request
units.note: ask, and I will give it to you

verses.text: That night God appeared to Solomon and said, "Ask, and I will give it to you!"
Solomon replied to God: "You have shown much {{chesed|loving devotion}} to my father David, and You have made me king in his place.
Now, O LORD God, let Your promise to my father David be fulfilled. For You have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth.
Now grant me {{chokmah|wisdom}} and {{daat|knowledge}}, so that I may lead this people. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?"

units.label: God's answer and gift
units.note: wisdom and knowledge granted, riches besides

verses.text: God said to Solomon, "Since this was in your heart instead of requesting riches or wealth or honor for yourself or death for your enemies, and since you have not even requested long life but have asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern My people over whom I have made you king,
therefore wisdom and knowledge have been granted to you. And I will also give you riches and wealth and honor unlike anything given to the kings before you or after you."
So Solomon went to Jerusalem from the high place in Gibeon, from before the Tent of Meeting, and he reigned over Israel.

units.label: Solomon's wealth and power
units.note: silver and gold as common as stones

verses.text: Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills.
Solomon's horses were imported from Egypt and Kue, the royal merchants purchased them from Kue.
A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty. Likewise, they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram.

ohel.gloss: Tent of Meeting, the tabernacle Moses made in the wilderness. Before the temple is even begun, Solomon and all Israel gather to worship at this older, portable dwelling place of God, showing that the coming temple stands in continuity with the wilderness worship of the exodus generation, not as a replacement for God's presence but as its next, more permanent home.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, covenant loyalty, steadfast love. Solomon grounds his prayer not in his own worthiness but in the chesed God has already shown David, the same word that anchors Israel's worship throughout Chronicles, above all in the refrain, His loving devotion endures forever.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, skill in living rightly and governing well. Solomon asks for chokmah not to be clever or admired but to lead God's people faithfully; this single request becomes the defining gift of his reign and the subject of the queen of Sheba's astonishment in chapter 9.

daat.gloss: Knowledge, discernment. Paired with chokmah throughout the chapter, daat is the practical grasp of how things truly are, so that Solomon's rule would be shaped by reality and truth rather than guesswork or flattery.

basic.context: Solomon has just become king, and before he builds a single wall of the temple, he leads all Israel to worship at Gibeon, where the old tabernacle from the wilderness still stood. There God appears to him at night and makes an astonishing offer, ask for anything. Solomon, remembering God's loving devotion to his father David, asks not for riches or long life but for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people well. God is so pleased with this request that He grants it, and then adds unmatched wealth and honor besides.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historical encounter that launches Solomon's reign, not a general promise that God grants any believer's request. What is timelessly true is the pattern: those who seek God's kingdom and the good of others above their own advantage find that God supplies far more than they asked. The chapter also quietly shows how good beginnings can still end badly, since this same Solomon's chariots, horses, and gold, the very things later kings are warned against multiplying, Deuteronomy 17:16 to 17, will one day contribute to his downfall.
basic.originalLanguages: Solomon appeals to God's chesed, His loving devotion to David, before asking for chokmah and daat, wisdom and knowledge, to govern well. The pairing of these two Hebrew words describes not mere cleverness but a discerning grasp of how to lead God's people according to His truth, the very gift Israel's wisdom literature and, finally, Christ Himself embody.
basic.typology: Solomon at prayer before the tabernacle, asking for wisdom to shepherd God's people, foreshadows the greater Son of David in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, Colossians 2:3. Where Solomon's wisdom was granted and later compromised by the very riches God added, Christ's wisdom never fails and never turns Him from His Father.
basic.christ: Solomon is called wiser than any king before or after him, yet Scripture points to one greater than Solomon, Matthew 12:42, in whom wisdom is not merely given but who is Himself the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30. Solomon prayed for wisdom to govern a single nation for a lifetime; Christ possesses perfect wisdom to govern an everlasting kingdom of every nation.
basic.god: God delights to give generously to those who ask according to His purposes rather than their own comfort. He keeps covenant loyalty across generations, honoring His promise to David through Solomon, and He is willing to be sought, appearing to Solomon at night simply because Solomon and Israel had first come to seek Him at Gibeon.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 3 gives the parallel account of this same night at Gibeon. James 1:5 promises wisdom to whoever asks God in faith. Matthew 6:33 teaches that seeking God's kingdom first brings every other good thing besides. And Colossians 2:3 declares that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
basic.oneStory: At the very start of his reign, Solomon shows what a heart rightly ordered toward God looks like: worship first, then a request for wisdom to serve others rather than riches to serve himself. God's generous answer, wisdom granted and wealth added besides, previews the pattern Jesus later teaches, seek first the kingdom, and anticipates the true Solomon, Christ, in whom the fullness of wisdom dwells for the good of His people forever.

context.literary:
Chapter one opens a frame that will not close until chapter nine. Verse one's report that the LORD had highly exalted him answers 1 Chronicles 29:25, where the Chronicler had already told his readers, at David's death, that the LORD highly exalted Solomon in the sight of Israel and bestowed on him royal splendor beyond any king before him. Chapter one therefore begins by fulfilling a promise its readers already know is coming; nothing here is a surprise so much as a confirmation.

The assembly of verse two, Solomon summoning commanders, judges, and family heads, deliberately imitates his father's practice in 1 Chronicles 28 and 29 of gathering all Israel before undertaking the temple project. Solomon's first act as sole king is corporate worship, not private ambition, a pattern the Chronicler wants his own fractured, kingless community to notice and copy.

The chapter's geography is also doing narrative work. The ark rests under a tent in Jerusalem while the altar and tabernacle remain at Gibeon, a divided arrangement the passage states plainly and never resolves; that unresolved split becomes the very problem the temple, still several chapters away, is built to solve. Framing the whole scene are two numerical excesses, a thousand burnt offerings at the opening and an empire's worth of chariots, horses, and silver at the close, both functioning rhetorically to establish scale before the greater scale of the temple's own gold and bronze is even described.
context.historical:
Gibeon lay only a few miles northwest of Jerusalem, close enough that the procession described here could be completed within a single day, unlike the earlier journey of the ark itself from Kiriath-jearim, where it had rested for roughly twenty years after its return from Philistine captivity, 1 Samuel 7:1-2, before David finally brought it up. Gibeon was itself a Levitical town, Joshua 21:17, and 1 Chronicles 16:39-40 records that Zadok the priest and his colleagues ministered continually before the tabernacle there even while other priests and singers served the ark in Jerusalem, an arrangement that explains why the whole assembly had reason to travel rather than simply worship at home.

The bronze altar named in verse five was not newly made; it traced back, through the notice that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had built it, to the original wilderness craftsmen of Exodus 31:1-11, anchoring Solomon's worship to equipment already several centuries old. The horse and chariot trade of verses fourteen through seventeen situates Solomon within a wider tenth century commercial network; Kue, in Cilicia, and Egypt were both recognized sources of horses in the ancient Near East, and Solomon's court functioned as a middleman, buying from one region and reselling to Hittite and Aramean kings further north and east, a level of international commerce unmatched by any previous Israelite king.
context.canonical:
By the time a reader reaches 2 Chronicles 1, 1 Chronicles 29:25 has already announced that the LORD highly exalted Solomon; the opening verse here simply confirms what the end of the previous book promised, binding the two books together as a single continuous account rather than a fresh start. The invitation of verse seven, ask, and I will give it to you, echoes the language of Psalm 2:8, where the LORD tells His anointed king, ask of Me, and I will make the nations your heritage, a royal coronation psalm that later readers applied to great David's greater Son.

Chronicles is also notably silent here about something 1 Kings places at the very start of the Gibeon episode, Solomon's marriage alliance with Pharaoh's daughter, 1 Kings 3:1. The Chronicler does not suppress this marriage forever; he simply relocates its mention to 2 Chronicles 8:11, well after the temple stands finished, so that nothing clouds the unhurried, wholehearted devotion of these opening chapters. Nehemiah 9:20 later thanks God for giving His good Spirit to instruct the returning generation, and Isaiah 11:2 promises a future branch from Jesse resting under the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, both texts reading backward into this very gift as a pattern of what God's chosen leaders are given to receive.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Chronicler's first readers had watched a line of kings end in defeat and exile; they had no standing throne and no guarantee that Davidic kingship would ever return. By opening Solomon's reign with security that comes from worship rather than warfare, verse one's established himself securely arriving in the same breath as an act of corporate sacrifice, the author wants that community to see where true stability comes from even without a king of their own.

He also intends a contrast most ancient readers would catch instantly. Saul, whose very name means asked for, never received an invitation from God to ask for anything, and later sought answers from a medium instead, 1 Samuel 28. Solomon is handed the invitation Saul never received and uses it rightly. The author is teaching his exilic audience two ways of asking, one that grasps for security on its own terms and one that waits to be invited and then requests what serves others, and he wants them to choose the second even while they wait, like Solomon before the temple existed, without a finished house of their own.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in this chapter instructs believers to travel to a particular holy site or expect a night vision as the normal means of receiving wisdom from God; that specific, unrepeated form belongs to the historical description of how God chose to equip one king at one moment. What carries forward as pattern rather than one time event is the shape of the whole scene, gathering God's people around a major decision before acting alone, verse two, grounding a request in what God has already done rather than personal merit, verses eight and nine, and asking for the capacity to serve others rather than to be served.

Jesus reissues that priority as a general command open to any disciple, seek first the kingdom of God, Matthew 6:33, and James removes even the kingly restriction, promising wisdom to any of you who asks in faith, James 1:5. What must not be prescribed from this text is the idea that ask, and I will give it to you, verse seven, functions as a blank check detached from Solomon's God centered and others serving content; the promise was never a formula, and the chapter's own sequel shows how wealth, rightly granted, can still become a snare when it outgrows its original purpose.

debates.question: Why does the Chronicler open Solomon's reign with worship at Gibeon rather than with the succession struggle found in 1 Kings 1 and 2?

views.label: A deliberately idealized portrait for a hopeful audience
views.case: Writing to exiles who needed a pattern to imitate rather than a full political history, the Chronicler omits Adonijah's rival claim, Joab's execution, and Shimei's death, and instead opens with unclouded worship and a selfless request, presenting the best of Solomon as an example rather than a complete biography of his rise to power.

views.label: A theological rather than chronological priority built into the whole book
views.case: Throughout both books of Chronicles, the author consistently subordinates political detail to worship and temple concerns; the same pattern shapes his account of David, where census and conquest matter far less than the ark and the sacrifices. Opening with Gibeon signals from the first verse that everything Solomon will accomplish flows from seeking God first, a structural choice repeated at the start of nearly every reign in the book.

debates.bearing: Both explanations agree that the arrangement is deliberate rather than incomplete; the Chronicler wants a community without a king of its own to measure faithfulness by worship and priority, not by political survival.

debates.question: Why does Solomon ask for wisdom and knowledge, verse ten, where the parallel account in 1 Kings 3:9 has him ask instead for an understanding heart to judge?

views.label: Synonymous parallelism, no substantive difference
views.case: Hebrew narrative often pairs near synonyms for rhetorical fullness, and the two accounts describe the same single request from two angles; nothing in the wider context suggests Solomon asked for two separate things or that Kings and Chronicles disagree about what was actually requested.

views.label: A deliberate link to the building competence the next chapter requires
views.case: Chronicles alone will use closely related language again in chapter two to describe Huram-abi's God given skill for constructing the temple; read together, the double term here anticipates that the wisdom granted to Solomon is not confined to the judicial rulings later shown in 1 Kings 3:16-28 but extends to the practical competence needed for the building project that occupies the very next chapter, a connection unique to the Chronicler's arrangement of the material.

debates.bearing: Either way, the request is broader than legal judgment alone; Chronicles, more than Kings, positions this gift as the wisdom that will shortly gather craftsmen, materials, and a workforce capable of raising the temple itself.

study.originalLanguages:
Five features of the Hebrew text reward closer attention beyond the chesed, chokmah, and daat already named. Verse one opens with a reflexive verb, wayyitchazzeq, from chazaq, to be strong; the hitpael stem means Solomon strengthened himself, an active, reflexive sense that sits immediately beside the passive claim that the LORD exalted him. The verse holds both truths in a single breath, human resolve and divine gift, without resolving which comes first.

The verb translated highly exalted is a form of gadal, to grow great or magnify; the same root appears in 1 Chronicles 29:25 describing how the LORD magnified Solomon in the eyes of all Israel. Chronicles uses gadal sparingly and almost always of what God does to a person rather than what a person achieves alone, so its appearance here at the very start of the reign functions as a quiet claim about the source of Solomon's greatness before a single accomplishment is narrated.

The pivot of the whole scene is the verb sha'al, to ask, repeated in God's offer, verse seven, and in the narrator's summary of what Solomon did not ask for, verse eleven. The same root gives the name Sha'ul, Saul, meaning asked for, a coincidence worth noticing precisely because Saul in his own reign never received such an invitation and later sought an answer from a medium at Endor rather than from the LORD, 1 Samuel 28. Solomon receives the invitation Saul never did, and asks well.

God's evaluation in verse eleven turns on the phrase since this was in your heart, using lebab, heart, the Hebrew center of decision and intention rather than mere emotion. God is shown weighing the root motive behind Solomon's words, not simply cataloguing the words themselves, a distinction Chronicles will return to often when it measures kings by the condition of the heart rather than the success of their projects.

Finally, the BSB footnote on verse ten preserves an idiom the translation smooths over. Literally, Solomon asks so that he may go out before this people and come in, an expression for competent leadership found also in Numbers 27:17, where Moses asks the LORD to appoint someone who will go out and come in before them, and in Deuteronomy 31:2, where Moses describes his own inability to do the same at a hundred and twenty years old. Solomon's abstract request for wisdom and knowledge is therefore anchored in a very concrete picture, a king capable of leading armies out to battle and bringing the nation safely home again, the daily competence a shepherd of God's flock actually needs.

typology.type: Solomon summoned before God at night with an open invitation to ask, verse seven
typology.fulfillment: Jesus later issues the same invitation without restriction of throne or nation. Whoever abides in Him may ask whatever they wish, John 15:7, and may ask the Father directly in His name, John 16:23-24. Solomon's audience came once, to one king, through a dream at a specific altar; Christ's invitation is repeated, standing, and open to every disciple at any hour. The correspondence still falls short in one direction, since Solomon's asking, however wise, remained bounded by his own understanding, while believers ask in the name of one who already knows the Father's will perfectly and intercedes for them, Hebrews 7:25.

typology.type: Wisdom and knowledge granted, with riches and honor added beyond what was requested, verses eleven and twelve
typology.fulfillment: Jesus makes this very sequence a general teaching rather than a royal exception, seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you, Matthew 6:33. Solomon received the addition because he asked rightly for a single reign; every disciple who seeks God's kingdom first is promised the same generous excess, though what is added will not always be silver and gold. The pattern escalates in Christ because the kingdom now sought is not Israel's throne but an everlasting one that outlasts every treasury, however full.

typology.type: The question who is able to govern this great people, verse ten
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's honest admission of insufficiency before an enormous task anticipates the promise of a coming ruler on whose shoulders government itself will finally rest without strain, Isaiah 9:6-7, whose increase of peace and justice will have no end. Solomon's wisdom, however real, still needed constant replenishing and eventually failed him in his old age; the government Isaiah promises never needs to be asked for twice, because it is given once, permanently, to one who never depended on inherited wealth or foreign alliance to sustain it.

study.christ:
This chapter reaches toward Christ along three separate lines. First, the invitation itself. God's word to Solomon, ask, and I will give it to you, verse seven, was spoken once, at night, to one king, at a specific altar that no longer exists. Jesus turns the same offer into a standing promise for every disciple, if you abide in Me, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you, John 15:7, and in that day you will ask in My name, John 16:23-24. What was extraordinary and unrepeatable for Solomon becomes ordinary and repeated for anyone united to Christ.

Second, the trade in horses and chariots that closes the chapter, verses fourteen through seventeen, quietly anticipates a contrast the Gospels make explicit. Solomon multiplied exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16 had warned a king not to multiply, and did so as a mark of prestige and security. When great David's greater Son enters His own city to claim His kingdom, He comes not multiplying warhorses for Himself but riding a borrowed colt, deliberately fulfilling Zechariah 9:9-10 as Matthew notes, Matthew 21:5, a king whose reign advances by humility rather than military stockpile. Only when He returns in final judgment does Revelation picture Him on a white horse, and even then the armies that follow Him are clothed in fine linen, not armed for commercial advantage, Revelation 19:11-14.

Third, Solomon's own honest question, who is able to govern this great people, verse ten, finds its answer not in a wiser version of Solomon but in a different kind of king altogether. Isaiah promises a child who will bear the government on His own shoulder, whose wisdom will not need to be requested because it is His very identity, Wonderful Counselor, and whose increase of government and peace will have no end, Isaiah 9:6-7. Solomon governed one nation for one lifetime and needed wisdom granted to him from outside himself; Christ governs an everlasting kingdom of every nation as wisdom itself, needing nothing added, and yet inviting His people to ask Him for it freely, exactly as the Father once invited Solomon.
study.god:
God's generosity in this chapter is not generic; it is aimed with precision at the actual content of a heart. Verse eleven has God itemize, almost like a ledger, exactly what Solomon did not ask for, riches, wealth, honor, the death of his enemies, even long life, before naming what he did ask for. This is not God assuming the worst of a young king and being pleasantly surprised; it is God reading the heart behind the request and responding to what He finds there, the same discernment the Chronicler will later state as a settled principle, the eyes of the LORD roam throughout the earth to show Himself strong for those whose hearts are fully His, 2 Chronicles 16:9. This chapter is the first exhibit of that later claim.

God's initiative also runs ahead of Solomon's asking. Nothing in verses one through six records Solomon requesting an audience or a vision; he and the assembly simply worship, offering sacrifices at the ancient altar. God is the one who appears, unprompted, that night, turning ordinary worship into an extraordinary encounter no one had engineered. Grace, in other words, precedes even the granted request; the whole scene begins with God showing up before anyone asks Him to.

God is also shown holding together immense freedom and immense faithfulness at once. He extends the widest possible invitation, ask for anything, with no stated limit, and yet He is simultaneously the God who is keeping a specific, decades old promise to David, verse nine. His generosity is never arbitrary; it always flows inside the channel of a covenant He has already committed to keep. And He gives extravagantly beyond the request itself, not because Solomon negotiated for more but because open handed generosity is simply what God does when a request pleases Him, a pattern worth remembering whenever what is asked for seems, on the surface, to be too small to matter to Him.

crossReferences.note: The fuller parallel account of this same night at Gibeon, including additional narrative detail such as Solomon's earlier marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, 1 Kings 3:1, deliberately left out of the Chronicler's version so that nothing clouds Solomon's opening act of worship.

David's closing chapter already promises that the LORD would highly exalt Solomon before all Israel; 2 Chronicles 1:1 opens by narrating that promise's fulfillment in Solomon's very first act as sole king, binding the two books into one continuous story.

The LORD's coronation promise to His anointed king, ask of Me, and I will make the nations your heritage, supplies the royal background for God's open invitation to Solomon, and later readers heard the same promise reaching toward great David's greater Son.

Torah's king law specifically warns a future king not to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold for himself; the chariot and horse trade closing this chapter, however genuinely a gift from God, sits uneasily beside this warning and foreshadows Solomon's later compromise.

Moses asks the LORD to appoint a leader who can go out and come in before the people, the same idiom for competent leadership that lies literally behind Solomon's request in verse ten, smoothed into wisdom and knowledge by most English translations.

Saul, whose own name means asked for, never receives an invitation from God like Solomon's and instead seeks an answer from a medium at Endor when the LORD will not respond to him, a sobering contrast between two kings and two kinds of asking.

Any believer who lacks wisdom may ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, extending to every ordinary disciple the same invitation once reserved for a king at a specific altar in a specific century.

Jesus turns Solomon's experience, wisdom sought first and riches added besides, into a general command for every disciple, seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you as well.

Paul locates all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, the very gift Solomon requested and received only in part, hidden in Christ Himself, so that what Solomon received on loan for a lifetime, believers now possess by being united to Him.

Later in the book, every king of the earth is said to seek Solomon's presence to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart, confirming within Chronicles' own narrative that the request of chapter one was answered beyond dispute.

study.oneStory:
This scene sits at a hinge in the larger story of wisdom in Scripture. In the garden, the first man and woman reached for wisdom on their own terms, believing the fruit was to be desired for making one wise, Genesis 3:6, and grasped rather than asked. Centuries later, standing before the same God at Gibeon, Solomon does the opposite, offered anything he could name, he asks rather than grasps, wanting wisdom to serve others rather than to elevate himself, and it is given to him freely, not stolen. The chapter quietly repairs, on a small and temporary scale, one piece of what Eden broke.

Yet the repair is only partial, and the passage does not pretend otherwise. The very wealth God adds as a gift, the horses, chariots, and international trade of the chapter's final verses, will resurface across Solomon's later years as exactly the kind of excess Deuteronomy's king law warned against, and by 1 Kings 11 his heart, once fully God's, is turned by foreign wives and foreign gods. A request answered perfectly at the start of a reign does not guarantee a reign that ends well; wisdom given is not the same as wisdom kept.

The larger story therefore keeps looking further ahead, past every king whose wisdom eventually failed, to one who is Himself wisdom without beginning or ending, in whom, Paul writes, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, Colossians 2:3. What Solomon received on loan for a single lifetime, Christ possesses as His very nature, and what Christ possesses He shares without measure, inviting the same open request, ask, and it will be given, Matthew 7:7, to every disciple in every generation, until the day His kingdom needs no more asking because it is finally, visibly, all in all.

quiz.q: Where did Solomon and all Israel go to worship at the start of his reign?

options.text: To the high place at Gibeon, the location of the wilderness Tent of Meeting, where Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings.
options.note: Verses 3-6 place the whole assembly at Gibeon before the old tabernacle.

options.text: To the newly built temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The temple had not yet been built; that is the whole reason Solomon is at Gibeon rather than at a completed house of the LORD.

options.text: To Solomon's palace to celebrate his coronation.
options.note: The chapter describes worship at Gibeon, not a palace celebration.

options.text: Nowhere in particular; the text gives no location.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly names Gibeon and the Tent of Meeting.

quiz.q: What did Solomon ask God for when given the chance to ask for anything?

options.text: Wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people well, rather than riches, honor, or long life.
options.note: Verse 10 records this exact, selfless request.

options.text: Riches and wealth to secure his throne.
options.note: God explicitly notes Solomon did not ask for riches or wealth, verse 11, though God granted them anyway.

options.text: The death of his enemies so his reign would be safe.
options.note: Verse 11 specifically says Solomon did not ask for the death of his enemies.

options.text: Nothing; Solomon made no request at all.
options.note: Solomon clearly asked for wisdom and knowledge in verse 10.

quiz.q: How did God respond to Solomon's request?

options.text: He granted the wisdom and knowledge asked for, and added riches, wealth, and honor unlike any king before or after.
options.note: Verses 11-12 record both the granted request and the added blessing.

options.text: He granted wisdom only and withheld any further blessing.
options.note: God granted wisdom, but the text explicitly adds unmatched riches, wealth, and honor as well.

options.text: He refused the request because it was too humble.
options.note: The opposite is true; God was pleased precisely because the request was selfless.

options.text: He gave Solomon long life instead of wisdom.
options.note: God specifically notes Solomon did not ask for long life, and grants wisdom and knowledge instead, not long life.

quiz.q: What does the chapter's closing report of Solomon's chariots, horses, and gold suggest when read alongside the rest of the Torah?

options.text: It shows both the blessing God added and, in light of Deuteronomy 17:16-17, the very things a king was warned not to multiply, a tension the Chronicler leaves for later chapters.
options.note: The wealth is a genuine gift, yet it foreshadows the compromises multiplied horses and wives will later bring.

options.text: It shows only unqualified blessing with no tension at all.
options.note: It is a genuine blessing, but Deuteronomy's warning against a king multiplying horses and wealth gives the report a deeper resonance the reader should notice.

options.text: It proves Solomon disobeyed God from the very start of his reign.
options.note: At this point Solomon is being blessed for a right request; the text does not present this moment itself as disobedience.

options.text: It has no connection to any other part of the Torah.
options.note: Deuteronomy 17:16-17 directly addresses a king multiplying horses, wives, and silver and gold, a clear connection.

quiz.q: How does Solomon's request for wisdom point forward in Scripture?

options.text: To Jesus, who is greater than Solomon and in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, and who freely gives wisdom to those who ask in faith.
options.note: Matthew 12:42, Colossians 2:3, and James 1:5 all draw this line forward from Solomon to Christ.

options.text: To the idea that wisdom is only available to kings and rulers.
options.note: The pattern of seeking and receiving wisdom is not limited to kings; James 1:5 extends it to any believer who asks.

options.text: To a warning that no one should ever ask God for anything.
options.note: The chapter commends Solomon's request; it does not discourage asking God for wisdom.

options.text: It has no connection to the rest of Scripture.
options.note: Multiple New Testament texts explicitly build on this theme of wisdom granted by God.

questions: Solomon worshiped before he asked for anything. What would it look like for you to seek God's presence first, before bringing Him your requests this week?
Solomon asked for wisdom to serve others rather than riches to serve himself. Where in your own life are you tempted to ask God for comfort rather than the ability to serve well?
God gave Solomon far more than he asked for. Where have you seen God's generosity exceed your own requests or expectations?

The chapter's closing list of chariots, horses, and gold hints at future compromise even in the midst of blessing. What blessings in your own life could quietly become a snare if you are not watchful?
Jesus is described as greater than Solomon, the very wisdom of God. What does it mean for you practically to seek His wisdom this week rather than relying only on your own understanding?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote records a textual variant: the Septuagint, Vulgate, and some Hebrew manuscripts read was there before, while the Masoretic Text reads he placed before; the difference does not affect the sense that the bronze altar stood at Gibeon.
Loving devotion renders the Hebrew chesed, translated in most places throughout Scripture with the same phrase; its range of meaning includes love, kindness, faithfulness, and covenant loyalty.
Kue is understood to be a region in Cilicia, in the southeast of Asia Minor, part of the international horse trade the verse describes.
